lesson.subtitle: Lesson 2 -- The Territory and the Team
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Renato Annunciato | Lesson 2 -- The Territory and the Team

listenings.text: People think we draw territories with a ruler, and we do not. If you split a country by area, you get one consultant with a beautiful map and no clients, and another one drowning in a city block. So we start from the other end. We count the clients who actually buy, we weight them, and only then do we draw the line. The second thing nobody expects is that the biggest territory is almost never the best one. The best territory is the one where the workload matches the person. I have seen a consultant lose half a region because somebody gave them more accounts than any human being can visit in a month. And the last thing. Every time we redraw a map, somebody loses a client they have known for six years. That part is not a spreadsheet problem, and if a manager treats it like one, the redraw fails, no matter how good the numbers look.

Two years ago I split my largest territory in half, and I got the sequence completely wrong. I announced the new maps on a Monday morning, in a group call, with the numbers on a slide. It was efficient and it was a disaster. Two of my best people spent the rest of the quarter wondering what the decision said about them. What I would do differently is simple, and it costs nothing. Talk to each person alone, before the group call, and tell them the reason first and the map second. The reason is almost always coverage. Nobody argues with the idea that a client who is visited twice a year is a client we are going to lose. What people argue with is a map that appears on a screen with no explanation attached to it. The split itself was right. We reached more clients that year than the year before, with the same headcount. It was the way I told the story that cost me two quarters of trust.

extra_audio.text: The Southeast is our largest territory, and it is more complex than the South. We allocate four consultants to it, because the workload there is heavier. The South is smaller, but the coverage is better than it was last year. Our benchmark is simple: every key account is visited at least once a month.

reading.rtitle: Territory Review -- South and Southeast, Brazil
paras: The commercial structure for Brazil is organised in two territories. The Southeast is the larger of the two and carries the heavier workload: four consultants cover Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Minas Gerais and Espirito Santo. The South is smaller, with three consultants covering Parana, Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul.

Coverage is measured as the share of key accounts visited at least once a month. On this benchmark the South performs better than the Southeast, at ninety-one percent against eighty-four percent. The difference is not explained by distance. It is explained by workload: the average consultant in the Southeast carries almost twice as many accounts as a consultant in the South.

The main gap sits in the interior of Sao Paulo, where reach is lowest and the backlog of unvisited accounts is longest. Headquarters has approved one additional position for the region, and the territory will be split before the end of the year. The new line will be drawn from the number of active accounts, not from the map.

Consultants will be ranked for the new allocation on three criteria, in this order: current coverage, growth in the last twelve months, and the size of the backlog they inherited. The manager will speak to each consultant individually before the structure is announced to the team.
